question: Can an unknown nonlinear instantaneous payoff in a continuous-time Nash differential game be inferred from optimal behavior by embedding the known dynamics, Euler-Lagrange/Pontryagin conditions, and a self-consistent control solver into a differentiable neural architecture?

key_findings.claim: Nash Neural Networks parameterize the unknown payoff and differentiate an augmented Lagrangian to produce state, costate, and stationarity equations while solving the control input self-consistently.
key_findings.evidence: Given known dynamics F, the network represents V(theta,psi,kappa), forms L'=V+lambda·F and L=L'-lambda·dot(psi), and uses automatic differentiation to obtain dot(lambda)=-partial_psi L', dot(psi)=partial_lambda L'=F, and partial_kappa L'=0. A nested numerical solver supplies kappa_opt back to every branch, with implicit differentiation used to train through that solver at the imposed Nash locus theta=psi and k=kappa.

anchors.section: 2.1 Optimal Control and 2.2 Optimal Decision Making during Epidemics

key_findings.claim: For the chosen SIR game, the analytic first-order equations correctly separate what behavior alone can reveal from what requires costate dynamics.
key_findings.evidence: The generating payoff is V=-alpha(i) psi_i-beta(kappa-kappa*)^2. Stationarity gives kappa_opt=kappa*-[psi_s i(lambda_s-lambda_i)]/(2 beta); dot(lambda_s)=kappa_opt i(lambda_s-lambda_i); and dot(lambda_i)=alpha(i)+lambda_i. Consequently, kappa_opt constrains the control-cost derivative and dot(lambda_s), but contains no direct information about the infection term alpha(i) psi_i; the paper's behavior-loss model accordingly misses dot(lambda_i) by approximately alpha_0.

key_findings.claim: The advertised inference 'from observations of behavior' is not demonstrated: both training regimes require exact latent costates generated from the hidden payoff, and the richer regime also uses their derivatives.
key_findings.evidence: The paper assumes complete theta=psi, lambda, dot(psi), dot(lambda), and kappa_opt trajectories. Lambda is an input even for L_kappa, while L_kappa,lambda directly supervises dot(lambda). These costates are produced by solving the synthetic forward-backward system using the true utility and boundary conditions; they are not observable human behavior. The conclusion explicitly concedes that lambda 'will never be available in real-life' and postpones eliminating it to future work.

anchors.section: 3 Nash Neural Networks, training information and Equations 31-33

key_findings.claim: Calling the procedure unsupervised is misleading: it is utility-label-free inverse supervision, not learning without targets.
key_findings.evidence: No values of V are labels, but L_kappa is an MSE against labeled optimal controls plus a stationarity residual, and L_kappa,lambda adds MSE against exact costate derivatives. State/costate trajectories and the known SIR equations provide dense synthetic supervision. A precise description is physics-informed inverse learning without direct payoff labels.

key_findings.claim: A single equilibrium trajectory and first-order residuals do not identify the plotted payoff away from observed controls or states, so the reported functional recovery is an inductive-bias selection rather than a unique inverse solution.
key_findings.evidence: The loss observes partial_kappa V and, in the richer case, partial_psi V only on the sampled Nash trajectory. For any smooth fitted kappa_opt(theta), adding a small term a[kappa-kappa_opt(theta)]^2 leaves its value and all first derivatives zero on that trajectory while changing curvature and off-trajectory payoff values; analogous functions vanishing to first order on the finite sample set create unlimited alternatives. Appendix B correctly describes a gauge G'(t,theta) that preserves the full Lagrangian field, but it does not cover the much larger finite/on-manifold observational equivalence class used by the experiment.

key_findings.claim: Solving the stationarity equation does not certify an optimal control or Nash equilibrium for an arbitrary learned payoff.
key_findings.evidence: The architecture enforces partial_kappa L'=0 through a nested minimizer/residual, a necessary first-order condition. It supplies no second-order concavity check, global maximum comparison, best-response deviation test, equilibrium uniqueness result, or verification that the selected stationary branch is continuous. The generating quadratic is concave in kappa, but the unrestricted tanh payoff network need not be, and minimizing a stationarity residual can select a minimum or saddle of utility.

3 Nash Neural Networks, stationarity-residual loss and root-finder replacement

key_findings.claim: On three synthetic epidemic trajectories, behavior-only training visually recovers the quadratic control-cost term, while behavior-plus-costate training also visually recovers the linear infection-cost term.
key_findings.evidence: Separate data are generated for alpha_0 in {100,200,400}, beta=1, and kappa*=4. With L_kappa, predicted kappa, state dynamics, and dot(lambda_s) track the generator and Figure 4 resembles -beta(kappa-kappa*)^2, while dot(lambda_i) and psi_i dependence fail as expected. Adding dot(lambda) supervision yields visual agreement in Figures 5-7 and slopes near -alpha_0 where trajectory data exist.

key_findings.claim: The numerical evidence is qualitative and in-distribution, with no baseline, seed variance, noise test, or independent environment validation.
key_findings.evidence: All points come from the same analytic SIR generator, test points are held out from the same one-dimensional trajectories, and only the portion with infected fraction at least 10^-3 is used. The paper reports aggregate training/test objectives but no payoff RMSE, gradient error, policy regret, counterfactual rollout error, confidence intervals, multiple initializations, optimizer comparison, or competing inverse-control method. Claimed extrapolation varies kappa while holding theta on the training trajectory, precisely where neural completion is non-identifiable.

key_findings.claim: The reported objective values show that the richer inverse problem is materially harder, but they do not measure recovery of the payoff itself.
key_findings.evidence: After 120,000 Adam steps with a three-layer 200-unit tanh network, L_kappa train/test losses are 3.2e-6/3.3e-6, 3.2e-9/1.0e-6, and 1.7e-6/1.8e-6 for alpha_0=100,200,400. L_kappa,lambda values are 1.1e-5/1.5e-5, 7.9e-5/2.4e-4, and 1.2e-3/9.6e-4. These mix prediction and optimality residuals with unspecified normalization, so small totals cannot validate utility identity or counterfactual transfer.

key_findings.claim: The synthetic terminal costate condition is not derived from the objective stated in the paper, leaving the demonstrated game insufficiently self-contained.
key_findings.evidence: Section 2 derives lambda(t_2)=0 for a free terminal individual state under the integral-only utility. The experiment instead sets lambda(t_f)=(s_f,i_f), calling this a vaccination boundary condition and referring to prior work, but it never introduces or differentiates the terminal payoff that would generate a nonzero transversality condition. The data may be valid for the external epidemic model, yet the inverse problem as written does not fully specify it.

method.core_idea: Represent an unknown payoff with a neural network, embed it in the augmented Lagrangian of a known continuous-time control/game model, and train through a nested stationary-control solver so observed Nash trajectories satisfy the implied first-order state and costate equations.
method.mechanism: The population state theta evolves under known F, while an individual's state psi follows the same dynamics with its own control kappa. Lagrange multipliers lambda impose dot(psi)=F. Automatic differentiation of L'=V_phi+lambda·F yields a stationarity residual, a costate vector field, and the known state vector field. At theta=psi and population control equal to the solved kappa, an implicit differentiable minimizer supplies kappa_opt. One loss fits observed kappa plus stationarity; a second also fits dot(lambda). Payoff differences are plotted to remove an author-identified gauge term depending only on time and population state.
assumptions: Population and individual dynamics F are known exactly and differentiable.
All individuals are identical, fully rational, possess perfect information, and follow a Nash equilibrium represented by theta=psi and k=kappa_opt.
The instantaneous payoff depends on time, population state, individual state, and control but not independently on velocities or other latent variables.
A first-order stationary point of the augmented Hamiltonian can be treated as the optimal control without an explicit global or second-order check.
The relevant stationary-control branch is numerically discoverable, locally unique, stable, and differentiable with respect to network parameters.
Exact state, control, costate, and derivative trajectories can be supplied during training; the paper acknowledges that costates are not observable in practice.
The SIR equations are a correct behavioral environment model and infection/control costs are stationary over an episode.
The continuum of people can be represented by one identical representative agent against the aggregate state.
One trajectory per infection-cost setting sufficiently excites the payoff coordinates to support functional inference.
A smooth three-layer tanh network's extrapolation away from the observed control/state locus reflects the generating payoff rather than arbitrary inductive bias.
The chosen terminal costate values correctly encode an external vaccination boundary payoff not derived in the paper.
Synthetic noiseless forward-backward solutions are representative of real behavioral observations.
The payoff gauge discussed in Appendix B captures the practically relevant non-uniqueness, despite additional finite-data equivalences.
ADAM and the nested implicit minimizer converge to a useful joint local solution from one reported initialization.

techniques.role: Models an otherwise unspecified smooth instantaneous utility rather than a fixed feature-weight form.
Enforces known individual dynamics with costates and exposes Pontryagin/Euler-Lagrange derivatives.
Differentiates the learned payoff to produce stationarity and costate vector fields.
Numerically solves for the control that makes the learned first-order optimality residual stationary/root-like.
Backpropagates through the nested control solution using JAXopt implicit differentiation.
Evaluates population and representative-individual branches at equal states and controls.
Fits optimal controls plus the stationarity residual while leaving some payoff-state dependence unobserved.
Adds exact costate-dynamics supervision to reveal payoff gradients with respect to individual state.
Compares payoff differences so terms depending only on time/population state cancel.
Generates noiseless Nash trajectories and latent costates for three epidemic cost regimes.

evaluations.setting: Synthetic representative-agent SIR distancing game for alpha_0=100, 200, and 400 with beta=1 and kappa*=4
evaluations.metric: Trajectory plots, aggregate train/test inverse losses, and qualitative payoff slices
evaluations.result: The method fits the analytic Nash trajectories and produces payoff slices visually resembling the generating control and infection costs
evaluations.baseline: Ground-truth analytic generator only; no inverse-control, inverse-game, PINN, or generic neural baseline

evaluations.setting: Training with observed optimal control plus stationarity residual (L_kappa)
evaluations.metric: MSE-like composite objective and visual agreement of kappa, dot(theta), dot(lambda), and V versus kappa
evaluations.result: Train/test losses range from 3.2e-9 to 3.3e-6; kappa, dot(theta), and dot(lambda_s) agree visually, the quadratic control-cost slice is recovered, and dot(lambda_i) is wrong by the unobserved infection-cost contribution
evaluations.baseline: Exact solution plotted as solid curves, with held-out points from the same trajectories

evaluations.setting: Training with optimal control, stationarity, and exact costate derivatives (L_kappa,lambda)
evaluations.metric: Composite objective and visual agreement of state/costate dynamics and payoff slices
evaluations.result: Train/test losses range from 1.1e-5 to 1.2e-3; both costate components and the linear infection-cost slope are visually recovered where data exist, at worse fixed-step optimization loss than L_kappa
evaluations.baseline: Exact synthetic derivatives and payoff, not observable-data or competing-method baselines

evaluations.setting: Off-control evaluation at population states lying on each training trajectory
evaluations.result: Curves often follow the true negative quadratic beyond the observed kappa_opt values, especially for stronger distancing
evaluations.baseline: Known generating quadratic; no alternative consistent payoff ensemble to quantify non-identifiability

evaluations.metric: 120,000 training steps of Adam at 5e-5 on a 3×200 tanh MLP
evaluations.result: One reported configuration converges to small composite objectives on noiseless trajectory samples
evaluations.baseline: No seeds, convergence distribution, runtime, memory, ablation, solver sensitivity, or public checkpoint comparison

limitations: Author-stated: the current method requires costates lambda that will never be directly available in real applications; removing them is deferred to future work.
Author-stated: noisy measurements, a government player, and simultaneous inference of government and individual utilities are not studied.
Author-stated: payoff terms depending only on time and population state have no effect on individual first-order equations and cannot be recovered.
Author-stated: behavior-only supervision cannot recover payoff terms that do not couple to the control, as shown by the missing infection-cost derivative.
Reviewer-identified: the 'unsupervised' description obscures direct MSE supervision from optimal controls and exact costate derivatives generated by the hidden utility.
Reviewer-identified: first-order information on one equilibrium curve leaves infinitely many utilities observationally equivalent beyond the Appendix B gauge.
Reviewer-identified: no identifiability theorem, feasible payoff set, uncertainty set, normalization, or rank/excitation condition supports recovery of the true utility.
Reviewer-identified: the nested stationarity solver supplies a necessary condition only, with no concavity, second-order, global best-response, or Nash sufficiency check.
Reviewer-identified: the epidemic example is a representative identical-agent aggregate game, not evidence for heterogeneous multi-player nonzero-sum differential games.
Reviewer-identified: all data are noiseless and synthetic from the same assumed SIR equations and utility family; there is no real behavior or model misspecification test.
Reviewer-identified: held-out points lie on the same three one-dimensional trajectories, and the claimed extrapolation keeps population states on those trajectories.
Reviewer-identified: no inverse-optimal-control, inverse-game, PDP, or generic neural baseline is evaluated despite extensive directly related work.
Reviewer-identified: payoff recovery is assessed mainly by plots, without payoff/gradient error, policy regret, counterfactual rollout error, or confidence intervals.
Reviewer-identified: one architecture, optimizer, training budget, and apparent initialization are reported with no seed variance or solver/architecture ablation.
Reviewer-identified: reported composite losses mix differently scaled prediction and stationarity terms and do not establish recovery of V.
Reviewer-identified: the experiment's nonzero terminal costate condition is not derived from the integral-only objective presented in the paper.
Reviewer-identified: perfect rationality, perfect information, known dynamics, identical agents, and exact Nash play are especially strong assumptions for pandemic behavior.
Reviewer-identified: the code is mentioned as being written in JAX/JAXopt, but the paper provides no repository, data artifact, or reproducible configuration beyond prose.
failure_modes: A neural payoff can match every observed first-order residual while giving arbitrarily different counterfactual utilities and policies off the training trajectory.
The inner solver can converge to a non-root residual minimum, a wrong stationary branch, or a stationary control that minimizes rather than maximizes utility.
Small control noise can make numerical differentiation of costates unstable, overwhelming the payoff-gradient signal.
Misspecified epidemic dynamics can be absorbed into the learned utility, producing an interpretable-looking but causally false infection or distancing cost.
Unobserved costates make the current architecture unusable on the real behavior that motivates the method.
Treating estimated costates as labels can leak assumptions or the true payoff from the forward model into the inverse learner.
One equilibrium trajectory may not excite controls or state directions; weak-distancing alpha_0=100 already provides little information.
Multiple equilibria or discontinuous best responses can invalidate implicit differentiation and make the learned branch initialization-dependent.
A payoff that changes over time, differs across people, depends on expectations, or contains constraints cannot be represented by the assumed shared stationary V.
Positive affine rescaling and richer reward transformations can preserve behavior, so point estimates may convey unjustified cardinal utility meaning.
Training/test splits along one trajectory can show low error while failing under a new initial infection level, terminal time, policy intervention, or disease parameter.
A learned off-trajectory quadratic can be a smoothness bias of tanh/Adam rather than evidence that the true social preference was identified.
The unexplained terminal condition can bake external utility information into costates, making recovery appear stronger than the stated inverse problem permits.
Assuming all observed actions are exact Nash responses can turn bounded rationality, delays, or social constraints into spurious utility structure.
reusable_insights: Distinguish direct payoff labels, behavior labels, latent adjoint labels, and physics residuals when describing inverse learning as supervised or unsupervised.
For inverse control, report the entire equivalence or confidence set of rewards consistent with observations rather than one neural point estimate.
Test identifiability constructively by adding functions whose relevant derivatives vanish on the demonstrated manifold and measuring counterfactual divergence.
Separate stationary-condition fit from optimality: verify second-order conditions, unilateral deviations, and forward re-optimization under the learned payoff.
Use multiple environments, initial conditions, horizons, or interventions to excite distinct payoff directions and shrink reward equivalence classes.
Evaluate inferred utilities through counterfactual policy transfer, regret under the true generator, and trajectory prediction, not visual payoff similarity alone.
Treat unknown costates as latent variables constrained by a boundary-value problem, with uncertainty propagated into the utility posterior or feasible set.
Compare neural inverse-game models with parametric PDP/KKT, maximum-entropy IRL, feasible-reward-set, and behavior-cloning baselines.
Audit whether terminal adjoint conditions reveal hidden terminal objectives and state those objectives explicitly in the inverse problem.
Add noise, partial observability, bounded rationality, dynamics misspecification, heterogeneous agents, and equilibrium-selection stress tests before policy interpretation.
Publish gradient-level diagnostics: stationarity residual, costate residual, Hessian sign, branch stability, and sensitivity to initialization.
When plotting off-manifold reward recovery, overlay multiple independently trained consistent payoffs to reveal epistemic non-identifiability.
open_questions: Can lambda be marginalized or inferred jointly from only noisy state/action trajectories and terminal conditions without leaking the hidden payoff?
What is the exact equivalence class of continuous-time payoffs consistent with a finite set of Nash trajectories under this augmented-Lagrangian model?
Which combinations of interventions, initial states, environments, or player populations make a nonlinear payoff identifiable up to an explicit gauge?
Can the method return confidence bands or a feasible payoff set instead of one arbitrary neural completion?
How should second-order optimality and unilateral best-response tests be differentiated through for a valid Nash certificate?
What happens when the stationarity equation has multiple roots or the equilibrium branch changes discontinuously?
Does the method recover useful counterfactual policies under new disease parameters, vaccination times, or government interventions?
How robust is payoff inference to SIR misspecification, delayed observation, reporting bias, and boundedly rational or heterogeneous agents?
Can entropy-regularized or probabilistic response models improve identifiability while representing behavioral noise honestly?
How does N3 compare empirically with Pontryagin differentiable programming, inverse KKT, maximum-entropy IRL, and modern inverse-game confidence-set methods?
Can heterogeneous multi-player payoffs be learned at scale without imposing equality between individual and aggregate states?
Which terminal utility generates the experiment's vaccination costate boundary, and how much of the inferred payoff is determined by it?
Can active experimental design choose interventions that maximally shrink the payoff equivalence class while remaining safe?
Would learned utilities remain stable across random seeds and architectures even when all observed trajectory residuals are equally small?

competitive_landscape.title: Pontryagin Differentiable Programming: An End-to-End Learning and Control Framework
competitive_landscape.difference: Jin et al. differentiate Pontryagin's maximum principle to learn dynamics, policies, and objective parameters and validate inverse RL, system identification, and control on several high-dimensional robotic systems. N3 emphasizes a neural payoff and self-consistent stationarity branch at a representative-agent Nash locus, but evaluates only one low-dimensional synthetic domain and does not compare directly with PDP.
competitive_landscape.source_version: NeurIPS 2020 proceedings version, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33

competitive_landscape.title: Guided Cost Learning: Deep Inverse Optimal Control via Policy Optimization
competitive_landscape.difference: Finn, Levine, and Abbeel learn arbitrary nonlinear neural costs with a maximum-entropy/sample-based objective under unknown continuous dynamics and demonstrate simulated plus real robotic manipulation. N3 instead assumes exact dynamics and first-order rationality, avoids direct payoff labels, and targets a differential-game interpretation, but lacks comparable real-data and unknown-dynamics evidence.

competitive_landscape.title: Reward Identification in Inverse Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Kim et al. formalize reward equivalence and give necessary and sufficient identifiability conditions for deterministic maximum-entropy MDP models. N3 discusses only one full-field Lagrangian gauge and does not establish whether its trajectory observations identify the learned payoff, leaving its off-trajectory recovery claim theoretically unsupported.

competitive_landscape.title: Identifiability in inverse reinforcement learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Cao, Cohen, and Szpruch characterize all rewards producing a policy under entropy regularization and show how multiple discount factors or sufficiently different environments can recover rewards up to a constant. Their result foregrounds the ambiguity that N3's single-trajectory neural reconstruction leaves unmeasured and suggests concrete multi-environment remedies.
competitive_landscape.source_version: NeurIPS 2021 proceedings version, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 34

competitive_landscape.title: Identifiability and generalizability from multiple experts in Inverse Reinforcement Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Rolland et al. give necessary rank conditions for identifying rewards from experts with different environments or discounts and characterize when nonidentified rewards still generalize. N3 trains separate networks on one trajectory per alpha and provides neither an excitation/rank test nor counterfactual generalization guarantees.
competitive_landscape.source_version: NeurIPS 2022 main-conference proceedings version, Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35

competitive_landscape.title: Efficient Inverse Multiagent Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Goktas et al. formulate inverse game and inverse multiagent learning as generative-adversarial min-max problems, provide polynomial-time/sample algorithms, and evaluate a real electricity-market time series. N3 supplies a continuous-time physics-informed architecture but no complexity, sampling, or real multiagent evidence.

competitive_landscape.title: Inverse linear-quadratic nonzero-sum differential games
competitive_landscape.difference: Martirosyan and Cao analyze N-player LQ nonzero-sum differential games, prove convergence/stability for model-based and model-free algorithms, and explicitly generate infinitely many equivalent games matching demonstrated feedback Nash trajectories. Its restricted cost family contrasts with N3's neural flexibility, while its equivalence analysis exposes a missing requirement in N3.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning true objectives: Linear algebraic characterizations of identifiability in inverse reinforcement learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Shehab et al. provide computable linear-algebraic characterizations of several identifiability notions and show how reward features/prior knowledge change them. N3's unrestricted neural payoff has greater approximation capacity but no diagnostic for whether the data constrain that capacity.

competitive_landscape.title: Offline and Online Nonlinear Inverse Differential Games with Known and Approximated Cost and Value Function Structures
competitive_landscape.difference: Karg, Varga, and Hohmann compute sets of all equivalent cost parameters for nonlinear feedback Nash games, prove online convergence to those sets, and analyze approximation-structure error and excitation. N3's neural architecture is simpler and differentiable end to end, but reports one point estimate with no equivalence set, convergence theorem, excitation test, or approximation-error bound.

competitive_landscape.title: Decoding Rewards in Competitive Games: Inverse Game Theory with Entropy Regularization
competitive_landscape.difference: Liao et al. explicitly address ambiguity and limited coverage in two-player zero-sum matrix and Markov games, establish entropy-regularized identifiability under linear assumptions, and return confidence sets containing plausible rewards with sample guarantees. N3 supports continuous state/control and nonlinear payoffs but neither quantifies ambiguity nor provides statistical guarantees.

competitive_landscape.title: Robust Inverse Reinforcement Learning Control with Unknown States
competitive_landscape.difference: Lian, Xue, and Nguyen infer quadratic cost weights and an optimal output-feedback controller from observable expert inputs/outputs despite disturbances and unknown states, with model-based/model-free convergence analysis. Their structural family is narrower than N3's neural payoff, but the observable-data and robustness guarantees directly address N3's acknowledged dependence on unavailable costates.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The paper presents Nash Neural Networks as a new physics-informed architecture that learns a general unknown payoff from rational Nash behavior by embedding classical-mechanics optimality equations and evaluating itself at a self-consistently solved control.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The full text derives the augmented-Lagrangian network, implements implicit differentiation through a nested control solver, and demonstrates qualitative payoff recovery on three synthetic SIR trajectories. Primary-source comparison shows that neural nonlinear inverse costs, differentiable Pontryagin/KKT learning, and inverse-game reward learning already existed; the most specific novelty is their wiring of a free-form payoff network, representative-agent Nash equality, and self-consistent stationary-control evaluation.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The architecture is a useful proof of concept for differentiable inverse optimality constraints, but the headline behavior-to-utility claim is not established because latent costates generated from the true payoff are required, first-order stationarity does not certify Nash optimality, and a single trajectory cannot identify the plotted off-path payoff. The defensible contribution is an implementation pattern and an observability demonstration, not general or uniquely identified utility inference.

reviewer_notes: Read all 14 cached pages, including Hamiltonian equivalence, payoff-gauge appendix, experimental figures, table, and references; checked eleven competing primary sources through official proceedings, OpenReview, or arXiv on 2026-08-23. The main non-identifiability audit is constructive: adding a small smooth term proportional to [kappa-kappa_opt(theta)]^2 changes off-trajectory payoff curvature while leaving its value and first derivatives zero on the demonstrated Nash curve, so neither loss can distinguish it there. This supplements rather than contradicts Appendix B, which analyzes transformations preserving the full Lagrangian field, not functions indistinguishable on finite/low-dimensional observations. The nonzero vaccination costate boundary may be justified by an external terminal utility, but that utility is absent from the stated objective, so it is recorded as under-specified rather than declared mathematically wrong. No generated projection was rebuilt.
